title: Architectural Conservation: Principles and Practice in India
author: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) & INTACH
topic: Lime mortar compatibility, stone masonry conservation, and non-destructive intervention
confidence_limitations: National guidelines establish authoritative policy standards and ethical boundaries, but do not replace site-specific petrographic, XRD, and moisture testing on historic stone/mortar samples.
practical_conservation_relevance: Provides regulatory basis for prohibiting Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) on historic lime masonry; mandates sacrificial breathability and minimum intervention.
non_generalizable_conditions: Not applicable to mid-20th-century reinforced concrete heritage structures.

title: INTACH Charter for the Conservation of Unprotected Architectural Heritage and Sites in India
author: Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH)
publisher: Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH)
topic: Indigenous master-builder traditions, vernacular craftsmanship, and minimum intervention ethics
relevant_region: Pan-Indian (special focus on vernacular and unprotected community water heritage)
confidence_limitations: Ethical and procedural charter; does not provide quantitative structural equations, finite element thresholds, or laboratory testing procedures.
practical_conservation_relevance: Affirms the priority of local traditional craftsmanship (e.g., Sompura, Chettiar, or local mistri guilds) and indigenous material systems over industrialized replacements.
non_generalizable_conditions: Guidelines do not supersede statutory safety evacuations when active structural collapse is imminent.
Traditional building knowledge must be verified for the specific regional geology before application.

title: Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India
author: Morna Livingston
topic: Stepwell typological evolution, subterranean microclimates, and stepped hydraulic access
relevant_region: Western and Northern India (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh)
confidence_limitations: Architectural and spatial documentation based on field surveys; lacks destructive core testing, chemical binder assays, and geotechnical pore-water calculations.
practical_conservation_relevance: Documents functional geometries of descending multi-tier galleries, structural pavilion cross-struts (kutas), and passive subterranean thermal buffering.
non_generalizable_conditions: Architectural configurations documented in semi-arid alluvial plains cannot be generalized to rock-cut plateau cisterns or wet tropical stepped tanks.
Assumptions regarding historical groundwater levels reflect pre-industrial water tables and must be recalibrated against modern over-extracted aquifer depths.
claim_supported: Stepped geometry enables direct, safe pedestrian descent to fluctuating seasonal groundwater levels across 10 to 25 meter ranges.
claims_supported: Stepped geometry enables direct, safe pedestrian descent to fluctuating seasonal groundwater levels across 10 to 25 meter ranges.
Subterranean tiered pavilions provide thermal dampening, keeping ambient temperatures substantially below exterior desert heat.

title: The Stepwells of Gujarat: In Art-Historical Perspective
author: Jutta Jain-Neubauer
topic: Vav subterranean architectural morphology, structural pavilions (kutas), and hydraulic design
historical_period: Solanki / Chaulukya to Sultanate periods (10th to 16th Century CE)
confidence_limitations: Primarily an art-historical and typological treatise; does not provide structural failure criteria, petrographic classifications, or hydraulic runoff modelling.
practical_conservation_relevance: Identifies the structural mechanics of kutas (multi-storey pillared pavilions) acting as retaining struts that counterbalance lateral soil thrust on long stepped corridors.
non_generalizable_conditions: Findings apply specifically to Gujarat vav typologies in alluvial soils; they cannot be generalized to basalt-rubble kunds of the Deccan Traps.
Orientation rules documented in historical texts represent ideal treatises (Vastu/Shilpa Shastras) and may vary based on local site topography.
claim_supported: The structural layout of Gujarat vavs incorporates multi-tiered pavilions (kutas) that counterbalance lateral soil thrust on stepped corridors.

title: Dying Wisdom: Rise, Fall and Potential of India's Traditional Water Harvesting Systems
author: Anil Agarwal and Sunita Narain (Eds.)
publisher: Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), New Delhi
topic: Traditional water harvesting typologies: Baoli, Bawari, Kund, Johad, and micro-catchment ecology
relevant_region: Pan-Indian (Thar Desert, Central Highlands, Deccan, Indo-Gangetic Plains)
confidence_limitations: Comprehensive socio-ecological and technical field survey; hydrological discharge figures and recharge estimates are representative rather than instrumented telemetry data.
practical_conservation_relevance: Demonstrates the necessity of conserving the complete hydrological ecosystem (catchment apron, feeder channels, silt traps) rather than treating the monument as an isolated architectural shell.
non_generalizable_conditions: Catchment revival recommendations assume available surrounding open catchment; severely encroached dense urban environments require engineered diversion retrofits.
Traditional runoff collection practices cannot be deployed without water quality testing in industrialized or pesticide-laden agricultural catchments.

title: Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen’s Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat - World Heritage Inscription Dossier
author: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) & UNESCO World Heritage Centre
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India
topic: Subterranean stepwell engineering, deep aquifer shaft mechanics, and structural conservation
confidence_limitations: Presents empirical conservation history of a single exceptional monumental site; foundation behavior under deep riverbed alluvium cannot be directly mapped to shallow bedrock stepwells.

non_generalizable_conditions: Subterranean hydraulic equilibrium observed at Patan reflects Saraswati river plain alluvial hydrology and does not apply to hard-rock Deccan aquifers.
Conservation techniques deployed for monumental state-protected sites may require adaptation for resource-constrained community-managed structures.

title: Handbook of Conservation of Heritage Buildings
author: Directorate General, Central Public Works Department (CPWD)
publisher: Directorate General, Central Public Works Department (CPWD), Government of India
topic: Traditional lime mortar preparation, surkhi pozzolanic ratios, and organic herbal additives
confidence_limitations: Standard field specifications based on historical PWD and ASI restoration protocols; exact durability of traditional organic additives (e.g. jaggery, urad dal) under modern acidic rain requires continued research.
practical_conservation_relevance: Provides standardized batching ratios for hydraulic lime-surkhi mortars, traditional slaking cycles, and wet-jute curing requirements.
non_generalizable_conditions: Fermented organic admixtures (jaggery, urad dal) must be avoided in poorly ventilated, stagnant subterranean chambers prone to biological fungal growth.
Mortar recipes must be adjusted based on the porosity and softness of the host stone (e.g., soft sandstones require higher sand/surkhi ratios than hard quartzites).

title: Traditional Water Harvesting Structures and Sustainable Groundwater Management in India
author: Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), Ministry of Jal Shakti
publisher: Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India
topic: Hydrogeology, unconfined aquifer recharge, and siltation dynamics in stepwells and tanks
relevant_region: Pan-Indian (emphasis on northwestern arid and semi-arid states)
confidence_limitations: Hydrogeological data based on regional observation well networks; site-specific recharge efficiency depends on local lithology, aquifer depth, and soil infiltration rates.
practical_conservation_relevance: Quantifies the barrier effect of bed siltation: compacted silt acts as an impervious hydraulic barrier, cutting off unconfined aquifer recharge and inducing stagnation.
non_generalizable_conditions: Stepwell recharge mechanisms only function if the structure intersects an unconfined or semi-confined aquifer with permeable strata.
Desiltation in contaminated urban areas must not be carried out without runoff quality analysis to prevent groundwater contamination.
claim_supported: Stepwells serve dual hydrological roles: groundwater extraction points during dry seasons and artificial recharge nodes during monsoon inundation.

title: IS 712: Specification for Building Limes
author: Civil Engineering Division Council (CEDC), Bureau of Indian Standards
publisher: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Government of India
topic: Building lime classification: Class A (eminently hydraulic), Class B (semi-hydraulic), Class C (fat lime)
confidence_limitations: Standard specifies properties for modern manufactured commercial limes; traditional historic field-slaked limes exhibit wider variations in unslaked residue, free CaO, and hydraulic index.
practical_conservation_relevance: Provides technical classification for specifying heritage mortars: Class A (hydraulic) for submerged water structures, Class B for structural masonry, and Class C (fat lime) for finishes.
non_generalizable_conditions: Class C fat limes cannot set in submerged or persistently damp underground masonry without pozzolanic activation (such as surkhi).
Standard values must be adjusted for historic soft lime putty aged in pits over multiple months or years.
claim_supported: Class A and B limes yield low modulus of elasticity (1.0-4.0 GPa) and moderate compressive strength (1.5-5.0 MPa) compatible with historic soft stones.

title: IS 3115: Specification for Lime Pozzolana Mixture
author: Civil Engineering Division Council (CEDC), Bureau of Indian Standards
publisher: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Government of India
topic: Lime-calcined clay pozzolana (surkhi) reactive blending and durability in hydraulic structures
confidence_limitations: Laboratory test specification based on standardized clay calcination; on-site crushed historic brick-bats may possess variable pozzolanic activity depending on original kiln firing temperatures.
practical_conservation_relevance: Verifies that reactive calcined clay (surkhi) binds free calcium hydroxide from lime hydration, producing insoluble calcium silicate hydrates (C-S-H) that resist water leaching while maintaining high vapor permeability.
non_generalizable_conditions: Over-burnt or vitrified industrial brick powder exhibits very low pozzolanic reactivity and cannot replace properly calcined clay surkhi.
Surkhi-lime mixtures require longer setting times than cement and must not be subjected to fast-flowing hydraulic wash during early cure.
claim_supported: Calcined clay (surkhi) reacts with free calcium hydroxide released during lime hydration, forming insoluble calcium silicate hydrates that resist water leaching.

Lime-surkhi blends provide vapor permeability (>15 Perm) far superior to Portland cement, preventing interstitial salt entrapment.

title: Historic Mortars: Characterisation, Assessment and Repair (RILEM TC 203-RHM)
author: P. Groom, J. Hughes, et al. (RILEM Technical Committee 203-RHM)
topic: Multi-dimensional compatibility criteria: mechanical, hygric, thermal, chemical, and reversibility
relevant_region: International / Arid and Temperate Heritage Environments
confidence_limitations: Peer-reviewed international consensus synthesis; specific physical constants and test protocols must be calibrated against Indian regional sandstones and traditional mortar admixtures.
practical_conservation_relevance: Defines multi-dimensional compatibility criteria: mechanical sacrificality (mortar weaker than stone), hygric vapor matching, thermal dilation compatibility, and chemical inertness.
non_generalizable_conditions: Test benchmarks developed for European calcareous stones cannot be directly applied to highly siliceous Indian quartzites without adjustment.
Reversibility criteria must consider that hydraulic lime-surkhi mortars achieve high final hardness over multi-decade carbonation.
